'''Marion Charlotte Thurnauer''' is an American [[chemist]] at [[Argonne National Laboratory]] (Argonne).  She was the first woman director of the Chemistry Division (CHM) and the first woman division director in the Physical Sciences Directorate at Argonne.  She is an Argonne Distinguished Fellow Emeritus in the Chemical Sciences and Engineering Division and has received numerous awards for her work in chemistry and her support of women in science.<ref name="Redacted"/>

==Early life and education==
Marion Thurnauer was born in [[Chattanooga, Tennessee]], later moving to [[Minnesota]]. Her father, Hans Thurnauer was a [[ceramic engineer]].<ref name=HansThurnaeur>{{cite news|title=In Memoriam, Hans Thurnauer, 1908-2007|url=http://www.electrochem.org/dl/interface/sum/sum07/su07_p20-21_25.pdf|accessdate=27 October 2014|work=Interface|issue=Summer 2007|publisher=The Electrochemical Society|date=2007}}</ref> Her mother, Lotte Oettinger Thurnauer, died in 1959, while Marion was still young.<ref name=HansThurnaeur/>   One of her aunts, Luise Herzberg, was an [[astrophysicist]]. Thurnauer credits family interests in science as a formative influence.<ref name = "Redacted"/>

She received her B.A. (1968), M.S. (1969) and Ph.D. (1974) in chemistry, from the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name = "Redacted"/><ref name=purple>{{cite book|last1=Hunter|first1=C. Neil|last2=Daldal|first2=Fevzi|last3=Thurnauer|first3=Marion C.|last4=Beatty|first4=J. Thomas|title=The purple phototrophic bacteria|date=2009|publisher=Springer|location=Dordrecht|isbn=978-1-4020-8814-8|page=xxxv|edition=Online|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZqlW5hEpAhAC&pg=PR32|accessdate=23 October 2014}}</ref>  Thurnauer credits her future husband, Alexander Trifunac with suggesting she study chemistry, rather than initially pursue her interest in biology, and learn the physical techniques of chemistry that could then be applied to biological systems.<ref name=Hinkle>{{cite book|author-last1=Keiter|author-first1=Ellen A.|author-last2=Piocos|author-first2=Elizabeth A.|chapter=Marion Thurnauer, Senior Scientist: A view from a government laboratory|editor-last1=Hinkle|editor-first1=Amber S.|editor-last2=Kocsis|editor-first2=Jody|title=Successful women in chemistry : corporate America's contribution to science|date=2005|publisher=American Chemical Society|location=Washington, DC|isbn=0841239126|pages=[https://archive.org/details/successfulwomeni0000unse/page/111 111–116]|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/successfulwomeni0000unse/page/111}}</ref>

Thurnauer's doctoral thesis advisor was [[Gerhard L. Closs]]. For her thesis work, she studied magnetic interactions in radical pairs using [[electron paramagnetic resonance]] (EPR).  The final experiments for her thesis research were conducted with an EPR spectrometer at Argonne because equipment at the University of Chicago had been damaged in an explosion.  Subsequent to this ‘unfortunate’ event she was offered a postdoctoral position in the Chemistry Division at Argonne.<ref name = "Redacted"/>

== Argonne National Laboratory ==
As a postdoctoral fellow at Argonne, Dr. Thurnauer worked with James R. Norris (chemist) and [[Joseph J. Katz]]. She used EPR [[spectroscopy]] to study photochemical energy conversion in the natural photosynthesis system. She was promoted to a staff position as an Assistant Chemist, and for several years was the only female staff scientist in the chemistry division.<ref name = "Redacted" /> From 1993 to 1995 she was the Group Leader for the Photochemical Energy Sciences Group.<ref name=Biography>{{cite web|title=Marion C. Thurnauer|url=http://www.cse.anl.gov/people/resumes/thurnauer_w_pic.pdf|website=Argonne National Laboratory|accessdate=24 October 2014|archive-date=14 October 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151014064815/http://www.cse.anl.gov/people/resumes/thurnauer_w_pic.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> From 1995 to 2003, she served as the first woman director of CHM, and the first woman division director within Argonne’s Physical Sciences Directorate.<ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Marion C. Thurnauer |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/thurnauer-marion-c|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name=Redacted>{{cite book|first=Hilary L. |last=Domush|title= Marion C. Thurnauer, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by Hilary L. Domush at Boulder, Colorado on 7 and 8 April 2010 |date=8 April 2010 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/thurnauer_mc_0674_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Science History Institute|Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref><ref name=Holl>{{cite book|last1=Holl|first1=Jack M.|last2=Schriesheim|first2=Richard G.|last3=Harris|first3=Ruth R.|last4=Hewlett|first4=Alan|title=Argonne National Laboratory, 1946-96|date=1997|publisher=University of Illinois Press|location=Urbana|isbn=9780252023415|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8-E0eK5VtRAC&pg=PA608}}</ref>  In 2003 she was recognized as an Argonne Distinguished Fellow. She is currently Argonne Distinguished Fellow Emeritus from the Chemical Sciences and Engineering Division.<ref name=Redacted/>  During her career she authored or coauthored more than 135 publications and was awarded 4 US patents.<ref name=staff>{{cite web|title=Staff: Marion C. Thurnauer|url=http://chmwls.chm.anl.gov/staff/photosynthesis/thurnauer.html|website=Chemistry Division|publisher=Argonne National Laboratory|accessdate=24 October 2014|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160124010205/http://chmwls.chm.anl.gov/staff/photosynthesis/thurnauer.html|archivedate=24 January 2016}}</ref>  She has actively encouraged other women scientists.

Dr. Thurnauers studies focused on the fundamental mechanisms of photophysics and [[photochemistry]] and their applications to the design of artificial photocatalytic systems.<ref name=Spectrum2004>{{cite journal|last1=Thurnauer|first1=M. C.|last2=Dimitrijevic|first2=N. M.|last3=Poluektov|first3=O. G.|last4=Rajh|first4=T.|title=Photoinitiated Charge Separation: From Photosynthesis to Nanoparticles|journal=The Spectrum|date=Spring 2004|volume=17|issue=1|pages=10–15|url=http://www2.bgsu.edu/departments/photochem/assets/pdf/spectrum/spring2004spectrum.pdf|accessdate=27 October 2014|archive-date=16 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221016112454/http://www2.bgsu.edu/departments/photochem/assets/pdf/spectrum/spring2004spectrum.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>  A major area of her research was solar photochemical energy conversion in bacterial and oxygenic photosynthesis and model photosynthetic systems.<ref name=staff/>  [[Oxygenic photosynthesis]] is the main process providing energy to the biosphere of the planet, creating the protective [[ozone layer]] and consuming [[carbon dioxide]].<ref name=Reza2013>{{cite book|last1=Razeghifard|first1=Reza|title=Natural and artificial photosynthesis : solar power as an energy source|date=2013|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc.|location=Online|isbn=9781118659892|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LQoFAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA49|accessdate=27 October 2014}}</ref> Photosynthetic organisms use solar energy, converting it into high-energy biochemical compounds.   With her colleagues, she modeled the spin and polarization of electrons in light-activated photosynthetic systems and helped to develop  time-resolved magnetic resonance techniques for the study  of sequential electron transfer in photochemical energy conversion. With her collaborators, she extended her concepts to bio-inspired nanomaterials that mimic the energy transduction of natural photosynthetic systems. She is a co-editor of  "The Purple Photosynthetic Bacteria" (2008), a collection of authoritative reviews on bacterial photosynthesis.<ref name=purple/>

== Women in Science and Technology ==
Dr. Thurnauer was awarded the Argonne Director’s Award for Extraordinary Effort in 1990 for her work in establishing  the "Science Careers in Search of Women" conference, an extremely successful program that enables students to learn about technical careers in science and engineering and meet with women working actively in science.<ref name=Holl/><ref name=Pacesetter>''Graduate School and Beyond: A Panel Discussion from the Conference Science Careers in Search of Women, Waterfall Glen Conference, April 6–7, 1989'', Argonne National Laboratory, 1989.</ref> The first year involved college women, but in ensuing years the program has worked with high school students.<ref name=Hinkle/>

After the second conference, Argonne leadership and women scientists launched the Argonne Women in Science and Technology (WIST) program.<ref name = "Redacted" /> Thurnauer and others emphasized that outreach and internal career development were closely linked, promoting change within the organization as well as without: "Young women could not be brought to Argonne and successfully encouraged to be scientists and engineers if they observed only a few women in relatively lower level positions."<ref name=Hinkle/> Thurnauer served a two-year term (1992-1994) as the Women in Science Program Initiator, a paid 30% appointment, and for several years was a member of the WIST Steering Committee.<ref name=Biography/>
